The dates of death of semisupercentenarians (age of death 105-109) starts at 1978. However, The data for supercentenarians only spans 1987-2024, so I truncate the dataset at 1987. This leads to a reduction of only 41 observations (15054 -\> 15013), which seems much too little. However, if you look at the death tallies for years shortly after 1987, you see that it's quite low. So probably it's not that bad.

```{r}
# Import the data
longevity_FR = read_excel("IDL_FRA_Death_105.xlsx") %>%
  filter(DEATH_YEAR >= 1987) %>%
  mutate(ltrunc = min(105, 1987 - BIRTH_YEAR), rtrunc = 2024 - BIRTH_YEAR)
```

```{r}
# Returns data truncated at age cutoff u
truncate = function(data, u) {
  filter(data, AGEYEARS >= u)
}

longevity_FR_supercentenarians = truncate(longevity_FR, 110)
```

## Some basic visualisation

Prima facie, it appears that the frequency decreases exponentially: the number of deaths at age t + 1 is about half that of age t, for all 105 \< t \< 115 or so.

```{r}
plot_histogram(longevity_FR)
plot_histogram(longevity_FR_supercentenarians)
plot_deaths_by_year(longevity_FR)
plot_deaths_by_year(longevity_FR_supercentenarians)
plot_yearly_maxima(longevity_FR)
```

Let's compare these with the expectation of the yearly maxes from a fitted model:-0.91

```{r}
fit1 = with(longevity_FR,
           fit_elife(AGEYEARS,
                     family = "exp",
                     thresh = 105))

fit2 = with(longevity_FR,
            fit_elife(AGEYEARS,
                      family = "gp",
                      thresh = 105))


# From AI:
gpd_max_mean <- function(n, sigma, xi, mu = 0) {
  stopifnot(xi < 1, xi != 0)
  mu + sigma / xi * (exp(lgamma(n + 1) + lgamma(1 - xi) - lgamma(n + 1 - xi)) - 1)
}

max_exponentials = function(theta, n) 105 + theta * sum(1 / (1:n)) # with shape parameter

plot_maxima = function(data, u) {
  gpd = with(data,
              fit_elife(AGEYEARS,
                        family = "gp",
                        thresh = u))
  
  sigma = coef(gpd)[1]
  xi = coef(gpd)[2]
  
  maxima = get_maxima(data) %>% 
    rowwise() %>%
    mutate(expectation_gpd = u + gpd_max_mean(DEATH_COUNT, sigma, xi))
  
  ggplot(maxima, aes(x = DEATH_YEAR)) +
    geom_point(aes(y = MAX_AGE, color = "Observed")) +
    geom_point(aes(y = expectation_gpd, color = "Expected_gpd"))
}

plot_maxima(longevity_FR, 110)
```

Despite the sharp, almost threefold increase in semisupercentenarian deaths over the period 20002-2024, the yearly maximum age at death seems more or less constant. Custom functions for data visualisation, for easy reuse at different cutoffs:

Threshold stability plot:

```{r}
with(longevity_FR_supercentenarians,
     tstab(AGEYEARS,
           family = "gp",
           method = "profile",
           ltrunc = ltrunc,
           rtrunc = rtrunc,
           plot.type = "ggplot",
           thresh = 105:110)
)
```

## Some basic model fitting

```{r}
null = with(longevity_FR,
            fit_elife(AGEYEARS,
                      family = "exp"))

MLE = with(longevity_FR,
            fit_elife(AGEYEARS,
                      family = "gp",
                      export = TRUE))


anova(null, MLE, test = "LRT")

plot(MLE, 
     which.plot = c("pp","qq"))
```
